i: In the quotation USD/INR = 84.10, which currency is the base currency?
Neither, because it is a cross rate
The first currency in a pair is the base currency; the quote tells how many units of INR (quote currency) buy one USD.
An Indian importer reads EUR/INR = 91.20, i.e. rupees needed to buy one euro. From an Indian resident's viewpoint this is a:
A direct quote expresses one unit of foreign currency in terms of the home currency, which is the norm in India.
In the interbank foreign exchange market, a standard 'spot' deal is settled on:
The fifth business day after trade (T+5)
The last business day of the month
The second business day after the trade date (T+2)
Spot FX conventionally has a value date two business days after the deal, giving time for cross-border payment processing.
A bank quotes USD/INR at 83.40 / 83.45. A customer who wants to BUY US dollars from the bank will be charged:
The bank sells USD at its ask (offer) rate, which is the higher side of the quote, i.e. 83.45.
If EUR/USD is 1.1000 and USD/INR is 84.00, the implied EUR/INR cross rate is:
Which feature is typical of an OTC currency forward but NOT of an exchange-traded currency future?
Contract terms are customised bilaterally between the two parties
Daily mark-to-market through a clearing corporation
Standardised lot size and expiry date
Forwards are privately negotiated and tailor-made, whereas futures are standardised, cleared and marked to market daily.
USD/INR spot is 84.00, the one-year INR interest rate is 7% and the one-year USD rate is 4%. Using covered interest parity, the one-year forward rate is closest to:
Under interest rate parity, the currency with the HIGHER interest rate will generally trade in the forward market at a:
Premium equal to its full interest rate
The forward rate offsets the interest differential, so the higher-yielding currency is cheaper forward, i.e. at a discount.
In a typical cross-currency swap, the two parties usually:
Exchange only fixed for floating interest in the same currency
Swap equity index returns for interest payments
Exchange principal at the start and end, and periodic interest, in two different currencies
Never exchange principal and settle only once at maturity
A cross-currency swap involves two currencies, so principal is normally exchanged at inception and re-exchanged at maturity along with interest flows.
An exporter expecting USD receivables in three months sells USD/INR futures today to lock in the rate. In this trade the exporter is acting as a:
The futures position offsets an existing business exposure, which is hedging rather than taking a fresh directional bet.
The standard contract size of a USD/INR futures contract on Indian exchanges is:
USD/INR futures are traded in lots of USD 1,000, keeping the contract accessible to small hedgers.
How are USD/INR futures contracts settled on Indian exchanges?
By physical delivery of US dollars
By delivery or cash at the buyer's choice
Exchange-traded currency futures in India are cash settled in INR; no foreign currency changes hands.
The final settlement price of an expiring USD/INR futures contract is based on:
The closing traded price of the futures on the last trading day
The USD/INR reference rate published (by FBIL) on the last trading day
The average traded price over the life of the contract
The rate quoted by the buyer's own bank
Final settlement uses the official reference rate on the last trading day, which removes scope for manipulating the closing futures price.
For monthly USD/INR futures, the last trading day is:
The last business day of the expiry month
The last Thursday of the expiry month
Two working days before the last business day of the expiry month
The 15th day of the expiry month
Expiry is set two working days before month-end so that final settlement aligns with the spot value date at month-end.
A trader buys 10 USD/INR futures contracts (lot USD 1,000) at 83.20. The day's settlement price is 83.45. His mark-to-market result for the day is:
JPY/INR futures prices on Indian exchanges are quoted in rupees per:
Because one yen is worth well under a rupee, JPY/INR is quoted per 100 yen to give a practical price.
An importer must pay USD 50,000 in two months and fears the rupee will depreciate. The appropriate hedge using USD/INR futures (lot USD 1,000) is to:
A USD payable is hurt by a rising USD/INR, so the importer goes long futures: 50,000 ÷ 1,000 = 50 contracts.

An exporter sells USD/INR futures at 84.00 to hedge receivables. At expiry the futures settle at 85.00 and he sells his dollars in the spot market at 85.00. His effective rate per USD is approximately:
He loses ₹1.00 on the short futures but gains ₹1.00 extra in spot, so the net realisation is 85.00 − 1.00 = 84.00.
USD/INR spot is 83.50 and the near-month future is 83.80. The basis, defined as spot minus futures, is:
The minimum price movement (tick size) in USD/INR futures is:
USD/INR futures move in ticks of 0.25 paise, i.e. ₹2.50 per tick on a USD 1,000 lot.
Exchange-traded USD/INR options in India are of which exercise style?
They can be exercised only on the expiry date, which is the definition of a European option.
A trader buys one USD/INR call (lot USD 1,000) with strike 84.00 for a premium of ₹0.30. At expiry the settlement price is 84.75. His net profit is:
The buyer of a USD/INR put with strike 83.50 pays a premium of ₹0.20. His break-even settlement price at expiry is:
A long put breaks even at strike minus premium: 83.50 − 0.20 = 83.30.
The maximum possible loss for the buyer of a currency call option is:
An option buyer can simply let the option lapse, so the worst case is losing the premium.
USD/INR spot is 84.20. A USD/INR put option with a strike of 84.50 is:
Worthless at any time before expiry
A put is in-the-money when the strike exceeds spot; here 84.50 > 84.20.
A USD/INR call with strike 83.00 trades at a premium of ₹1.40 when spot is 84.00. Its time value is:
Intrinsic value = 84.00 − 83.00 = 1.00; time value = premium − intrinsic = 1.40 − 1.00 = 0.40.
The 'delta' of a currency option measures the change in the option premium for a small change in:
Delta is sensitivity to the underlying price; vega, theta and rho cover volatility, time and interest rates.
In exchange-traded currency options, which party is required to deposit margin with the clearing corporation?
Neither party, since only premium is exchanged
The buyer's risk is limited to the premium paid upfront, whereas the writer has an open obligation and must post margin.
A trader expecting USD/INR to rise moderately buys an 84.00 call and sells an 85.00 call of the same expiry. This position is a:
Buying a lower-strike call and selling a higher-strike call creates a limited-risk, limited-reward bullish spread.
Ahead of a major central bank announcement, a trader expects a sharp USD/INR move but is unsure of direction. Which strategy suits this view?
Buying a call and a put at the same strike profits from a large move in either direction.
A trader buys a USD/INR 84.00 call at ₹0.50 and sells an 85.00 call at ₹0.15 (lot USD 1,000). The maximum profit on one lot is:
Max profit = (85.00 − 84.00) − net premium 0.35 = 0.65 per USD; × 1,000 = ₹650.
Selling a near-month USD/INR future and simultaneously buying a far-month USD/INR future is called a:
A calendar (time) spread uses the same underlying but different expiries.
An exporter wants protection against rupee appreciation but still wants to benefit if the rupee depreciates. The most suitable exchange-traded instrument is to:
A long put sets a floor on the rupee value of dollar receipts while leaving the upside open, at the cost of the premium.
USD/INR futures are trading well above their interest-parity fair value. An arbitrageur would typically:
Buy the futures and sell USD spot
Sell the futures and buy USD spot, funding it with INR borrowing
Selling the overpriced futures and carrying the cheaper spot position locks in the mispricing (cash-and-carry).
A trader buys an 84.00 USD/INR call at ₹0.40 and an 84.00 put at ₹0.35, same expiry. The break-even points at expiry are:
Total premium is 0.75, so break-evens are 84.00 ± 0.75 = 83.25 and 84.75.
A limit order to buy USD/INR futures at 83.50 will be executed:
Immediately at the best available price
Only at the day's closing price
A buy limit order sets the maximum price the buyer is willing to pay.
A stop-loss sell order with a trigger price of 83.20 becomes active when:
The market trades at or above 83.20
The market trades at or below 83.20
A sell stop order lies dormant until the trigger price is touched, then enters the order book to cap losses on a long position.
A Professional Clearing Member (PCM) in the currency derivatives segment is an entity that:
Trades only for its own proprietary account
Acts as the market surveillance regulator
Is required to quote two-way prices as a market maker
Clears and settles trades of trading members but does not itself trade on the exchange
PCMs, often banks or custodians, provide clearing and settlement services only.
Before placing derivatives orders for a client, a trading member must ensure the client is identified on the trading system through:
Exchanges require every client order to carry the client's registered UCC for audit trail and surveillance.
Novation in exchange-traded currency futures means that:
The clearing corporation becomes the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer
Trades are cancelled if prices move sharply
Buyer and seller must know each other's identity
Profits are paid only at expiry
By interposing itself, the clearing corporation guarantees settlement and removes bilateral counterparty risk.
Initial margin on currency futures is primarily designed to cover:
The potential one-day loss on a position at a high statistical confidence level
Brokerage and taxes on the trade
Losses over the whole life of the contract
Initial margin is risk-based (VaR-type) and sized for the worst likely one-day move, with MTM settled daily.
Daily mark-to-market profits and losses on currency futures are settled:
In cash, based on the daily settlement price
Futures are marked to market every day and the gain or loss is paid in cash, preventing losses from accumulating.
The main purpose of the Settlement Guarantee Fund maintained by a clearing corporation is to:
Ensure settlement is completed even if a clearing member defaults
The SGF is a pool of resources used to honour obligations when a member fails, protecting non-defaulting parties.
Why do clearing corporations generally charge lower margin on a calendar spread than on two separate outright futures positions?
Because gains on one leg largely offset losses on the other, so net risk is lower
Because spreads cannot be closed before expiry
Because spreads are not marked to market
Because the exchange guarantees spread profits
Near and far contracts on the same pair are highly correlated, so the combined position carries far less price risk.
Exchange-traded currency derivatives in India fall under the joint regulatory purview of:
FEDAI and the Ministry of Commerce
RBI governs foreign exchange and eligible participation, while SEBI regulates the exchanges and intermediaries.
RBI's authority to regulate who may participate in currency derivatives flows mainly from the:
FEMA empowers RBI to regulate foreign exchange transactions, including derivatives on currency pairs involving INR.
Which levy applies to exchange-traded equity derivatives but NOT to exchange-traded currency derivatives?
STT is levied on securities transactions such as equity F&O; currency derivatives are outside its scope.
For income-tax purposes, profits from trading currency futures on a recognised stock exchange are generally treated as:
Income from other sources exempt from tax
Eligible transactions in derivatives on a recognised exchange are excluded from the definition of speculative transactions.
SEBI's online platform where investors can lodge complaints against market intermediaries is called:
SCORES (SEBI Complaints Redress System) lets investors file and track complaints against listed companies and intermediaries.
Before a new client begins trading in currency derivatives, the trading member must provide the client with:
A Risk Disclosure Document explaining the risks of derivatives
The RDD is a mandatory part of client onboarding so that clients understand leverage and loss risks.
iv: When market yields rise, the price of an existing fixed-coupon bond:
Rises only if the coupon is high
Bond prices and yields move inversely because future fixed cash flows are discounted at a higher rate.
A bond with face value ₹100 pays an 8% annual coupon and trades at ₹95. Its current yield is approximately:
A bond pays a 7% annual coupon and the market yield for comparable bonds is also 7%. The bond will trade:
When coupon rate equals required yield, discounting the cash flows gives exactly the face value.
A bond has a Macaulay duration of 5 years and a yield of 8% (annual compounding). Its modified duration is approximately:
A bond has a modified duration of 6. If its yield rises by 50 basis points, its price will change by approximately:
Government of India Treasury Bills are:
Issued at par with half-yearly coupons
Issued at a premium and redeemed at a discount
Issued at a discount and redeemed at face value
T-bills are zero-coupon money market instruments; the return is the difference between issue price and face value.
Which of the following is NOT a standard tenor of Government of India Treasury Bills?
GoI T-bills are issued in 91-, 182- and 364-day tenors.
For an option-free bond with positive convexity, an equal rise and fall in yield results in:
A larger price loss when yields rise than gain when they fall
A larger price gain when yields fall than the price loss when yields rise
No price change in either case
Convexity makes the price-yield curve bowed, so price rises accelerate and price falls decelerate.
A bond with face value ₹100 pays an 8% coupon semi-annually. Using a 30/360 convention, 60 days have passed since the last coupon. Accrued interest per ₹100 is:
In a repo transaction, the party that sells securities with an agreement to repurchase them:
Permanently transfers ownership with no obligation
Is effectively borrowing funds against those securities
Is taking a short position in interest rate futures
A repo is a collateralised borrowing: cash is raised now and repaid on repurchase at a higher price reflecting interest.
A Forward Rate Agreement (FRA) is settled by:
Exchanging the full notional principal at maturity
Paying the difference between the agreed rate and the reference rate on a notional amount, without exchanging principal
Exchanging currencies at a fixed rate
FRAs are cash-settled on the interest differential applied to a notional principal.
In a plain vanilla interest rate swap, the two parties typically:
Exchange principal amounts in two currencies
Exchange equity returns for bond coupons
Buy and sell the same bond simultaneously
Exchange fixed-rate interest for floating-rate interest on the same notional in one currency
A vanilla IRS swaps fixed against floating payments; the notional is not exchanged.
In India's OTC market, the most actively traded overnight indexed swaps (OIS) are benchmarked to:
The floating leg of the dominant Indian OIS compounds the FBIL-published overnight MIBOR.
Exchange-traded bond (interest rate) futures in India use as their underlying:
Indian IRFs are written on GoI securities or T-bills, which are free of credit risk and widely held.
In a physically settled bond futures contract with a basket of deliverable bonds, the conversion factor is used to:
Adjust the invoice price for differences in coupon and maturity among deliverable bonds
Convert prices from INR into USD
The conversion factor standardises different deliverable bonds to the notional coupon so the invoice price is fair.
The cheapest-to-deliver (CTD) bond in a bond futures contract is the deliverable bond that:
Has the longest maturity in the basket
Gives the short the highest implied repo rate, i.e. the lowest net cost of delivery
Has the highest coupon in the basket
The seller chooses which bond to deliver and will pick the one that is cheapest relative to the invoice amount.
Bond futures settle at 98.00, the delivered bond's conversion factor is 1.05 and its accrued interest is ₹1.20 per ₹100 face. The invoice price per ₹100 face is:
If a bond's coupon yield exceeds the repo (financing) rate, the theoretical futures price of that bond will be:
With positive carry, holding the bond earns more than it costs to finance, so the futures price = spot − net carry.
A company with a floating-rate loan fears that interest rates will rise. Using an interest rate swap, it should:
Receiving floating offsets the loan's floating payments, leaving the company with a known fixed cost.
An FRA on ₹10 crore notional for a 90-day period has a contract rate of 7.00%; the reference rate fixes at 7.50%. Using Actual/365, the settlement amount before discounting is approximately:
Settlement = 10,00,00,000 × 0.50% × 90/365 ≈ ₹1,23,288, paid to the FRA buyer since the reference rate is higher.
A borrower with a floating-rate loan wants protection against rising rates while keeping the benefit of falling rates. She should buy an interest rate:
A cap pays when the reference rate exceeds the cap rate, limiting borrowing cost; if rates fall she still pays less.
An investor holding floating-rate assets who fears falling interest income would buy an interest rate:
A floor pays out when the reference rate drops below the floor rate, protecting minimum income.
An interest rate collar for a borrower is created by:
Buying a floor and selling a cap
Buying both a cap and a floor
Selling both a cap and a floor
Buying a cap and selling a floor
The sold floor's premium offsets the cap cost, but gives up gains if rates fall below the floor.
A call option on a bond price gains value when interest rates:
Become more volatile only on the coupon date
Falling rates raise bond prices, increasing the value of the right to buy the bond at a fixed strike.
A bank holding a large portfolio of government bonds fears yields will rise. To hedge, it should:
Buy a call option on bond futures
Rising yields cut bond prices; a short futures position gains as futures prices fall, offsetting the loss.
A portfolio has a PVBP of ₹42,000 per basis point and one interest rate futures contract has a PVBP of ₹140. The number of contracts needed for a hedge is:
Hedge ratio = portfolio PVBP ÷ contract PVBP = 42,000 ÷ 140 = 300 contracts.
A portfolio worth ₹10 crore has a modified duration of 6. Each futures contract has a value of ₹2 lakh and the futures' modified duration is 8. The duration-based hedge requires approximately:
N = (P × Dp) ÷ (F × Df) = (10 crore × 6) ÷ (2 lakh × 8) = 60 crore ÷ 16 lakh = 375.
A trader expects the yield curve to steepen, with long-term yields rising relative to short-term yields. A suitable futures trade is to:
Buy long-tenor futures and sell short-tenor futures
Sell long-tenor bond futures and buy short-tenor bond futures
Sell futures across all tenors equally
Long-tenor futures fall more if long yields rise relatively, so the short long-end/long short-end trade profits.
Bond futures are trading above their theoretical fair value. An arbitrageur would:
Sell the bond short and buy the futures
Buy the futures and buy the bond
Do nothing, since bond futures cannot be arbitraged
Buy the bond, finance it in the repo market and sell the futures
This cash-and-carry trade locks in the gap between the rich futures price and the carry-adjusted spot price.
An insurance company expects a large cash inflow next month for investment in bonds and fears yields will fall before then. It can:
This anticipatory (long) hedge gains if yields fall, offsetting the higher price it will later pay for bonds.
A trader expects the RBI to cut policy rates more than the market anticipates. A speculative position consistent with this view is to:
Lower rates push bond prices and bond futures up, so a long futures position profits.
A fund manager wants to raise the duration of a bond portfolio without buying more bonds. She can:
A long futures position adds interest rate sensitivity, effectively increasing portfolio duration.
Orders in exchange-traded interest rate futures are matched on the trading system on the basis of:
The size of the order only
The best-priced order executes first; among equal prices, the earliest order gets priority.
An Immediate-or-Cancel (IOC) order is one that:
Executes immediately to the extent possible, with any unfilled part cancelled
Stays in the system until the end of the day
Becomes active only when a trigger price is hit
Must be filled entirely or not at all on the next day
IOC orders do not rest in the book; whatever cannot be matched instantly is removed.
The main purpose of daily price bands or operating ranges on interest rate futures is to:
Prevent erroneous orders and curb extreme price moves
Fix the coupon on the underlying bond
Orders outside the permitted range are rejected or need confirmation, protecting against fat-finger errors.
An order that remains in the order book until executed, cancelled or the end of that trading day is a:
A day order is valid only for the trading session in which it is placed.
In exchange-traded interest rate derivatives, the clearing corporation substituting itself as counterparty to both sides of every trade is known as:
Through novation the clearing corporation guarantees performance, eliminating counterparty risk between members.
A trader buys 5 IRF contracts (face value ₹2 lakh each, price quoted per ₹100) at 98.50. The day's settlement price is 98.20. His MTM result is:
Loss per contract = 0.30% × 2,00,000 = ₹600; × 5 contracts = ₹3,000 loss for a long position.
Exchanges levy an extreme loss margin (or exposure margin) in addition to initial margin primarily to cover:
Losses from tail events beyond those captured by the initial margin model
Initial margin covers a VaR-type move; the extra margin buffers rare, larger moves.
If a clearing member defaults, the clearing corporation's first line of resources to meet the obligation is:
The defaulting member's own margins and collateral
The default waterfall uses the defaulter's resources first, before mutualised funds.
For a cash-settled interest rate futures contract, on the expiry day open positions are:
Settled by delivery of the underlying GoI bond
Closed out by paying or receiving the difference between the final settlement price and the previous day's settlement price
Rolled automatically into the next contract
Cash-settled futures end with a final MTM against the final settlement price; no bonds are delivered.
Under SEBI's margin framework, trading members must collect margins from clients:
Upfront, before or at the time of taking the position
Only when the client makes a loss
SEBI requires upfront collection of initial and exposure margins; short collection attracts penalties.
Which regulator issues directions on the OTC interest rate derivative products that banks may offer to their clients?
OTC interest rate derivatives involving regulated entities fall under RBI's directions.
OTC interest rate derivative trades in India are required to be reported to the trade repository maintained by:
CCIL operates the trade repository for OTC rate and forex derivatives, improving transparency for regulators.
Under the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, a 'derivative' includes a contract which:
Guarantees a fixed return to the buyer
Is issued only by the Government of India
Derives its value from the prices or index of prices of underlying securities
The SCRA definition centres on value being derived from an underlying, enabling exchange trading of such contracts.
Profits from trading interest rate futures on a recognised stock exchange are generally taxed as:
Short-term capital gains at a concessional rate
Eligible derivative transactions on recognised exchanges are excluded from speculative transactions under the Income-tax law.
Under Ind AS 109, an interest rate futures position that is not designated in a hedge relationship is measured at:
Fair value through profit or loss
Fair value through other comprehensive income only
Non-hedge derivatives are held for trading and their fair value changes go to the profit and loss statement.
Before onboarding a client for interest rate derivatives, a trading member must first:
Complete the client's KYC and registration process
Guarantee the client a minimum return
Take a position on the client's behalf
Obtain RBI approval for each client
KYC is a mandatory pre-condition for opening any trading account.
A trading member using one client's funds to meet another client's margin obligation is:
Prohibited, because client funds must be kept segregated
Permitted if both clients are related
Permitted for up to five days
Client money must be used only for that client's obligations; misuse breaches SEBI rules.
If an investor's complaint is not resolved satisfactorily by the intermediary, the investor can escalate it through:
SEBI's SCORES platform and the online dispute resolution mechanism
SCORES and the ODR framework are the designated escalation routes for securities market complaints.
viii: Basics of Derivatives
A derivative is best described as a financial contract whose value:
Is fixed at issue and never changes
Depends on the value of an underlying asset, index or rate
Depends only on the issuer's credit rating
Is always equal to the face value
Derivatives derive their value from an underlying such as shares, an index, currency or interest rates.
Basics of Derivatives
Compared with OTC derivatives, exchange-traded derivatives substantially reduce:
Market price risk
The need for any margin
Taxes payable on profits
Counterparty credit risk, because a clearing corporation guarantees settlement
The clearing corporation acts as central counterparty with margins and MTM, so participants do not depend on each other.
Basics of Derivatives
A participant who simultaneously buys in one market and sells in another to profit from a price mismatch is a/an:
Hedger
Speculator
Margin trader
Arbitrageur
Arbitrageurs exploit price discrepancies with little or no net market risk, helping align prices.
Basics of Derivatives
Which of the following is a key economic function of derivatives markets?
Transferring risk from those who want to avoid it to those willing to bear it
Raising long-term capital for companies
Guaranteeing returns to investors
Fixing the prices of underlying shares
Derivatives allow hedgers to shift price risk to speculators, besides aiding price discovery.
Understanding Index
The Nifty 50 index is constructed using which weighting method?
Price weighting
Equal weighting
Full market capitalisation including promoter holdings
Free-float market capitalisation weighting
Free-float weighting counts only shares readily available for trading, excluding promoter and locked-in holdings.
Understanding Index
A free-float index had a base value of 1,000 when the free-float market cap was ₹2,00,000 crore. If free-float market cap is now ₹2,50,000 crore (no corporate actions), the index value is:
Index = Base value × Current mcap ÷ Base mcap = 1,000 × 2,50,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 1,250.
Understanding Index
Impact cost of a stock measures:
The brokerage charged by the broker
The tax payable on a trade
The change in the index when the stock is added
The extra cost of executing a trade of a given size relative to the ideal (mid) price, reflecting liquidity
Lower impact cost means higher liquidity, which is a key criterion for index inclusion.
Understanding Index
A well-diversified, liquid index is preferred as the underlying for derivatives mainly because:
Its value never falls
It carries no market risk
It pays a fixed dividend
It reflects market-wide (systematic) risk and is harder to manipulate
Diversification removes stock-specific noise and makes manipulation of the underlying difficult.
Introduction to Forwards and Futures
A stock trades at ₹2,000. The risk-free rate is 8% p.a. (simple) and no dividend is expected. The fair price of a 3-month future is:
Introduction to Forwards and Futures
A stock is at ₹1,500, the financing cost for 2 months is 6% p.a. (simple), and a dividend of ₹10 will be paid before expiry. The fair value of the 2-month future is:
Introduction to Forwards and Futures
A market in which futures prices are higher than the spot price is said to be in:
Contango
Backwardation
Convergence
Inversion
Contango is the normal cost-of-carry situation where futures trade at a premium to spot.
Introduction to Forwards and Futures
As a futures contract approaches expiry, its basis (spot minus futures) tends to:
Converge towards zero
Widen steadily
Become exactly equal to the interest rate
Become permanently negative
At expiry the futures price must equal spot, so the cost-of-carry component shrinks to zero.
Introduction to Forwards and Futures
A trader buys one stock futures lot of 500 shares at ₹1,200. The day's settlement price is ₹1,185. His mark-to-market result is:
Profit of ₹7,500
Loss of ₹750
Loss of ₹15,000
Loss of ₹7,500
Introduction to Forwards and Futures
A portfolio of ₹1.5 crore has a beta of 1.2. An index future trades at 24,000 with an assumed lot size of 75. The number of contracts to sell for a full hedge is:
Contract value = 24,000 × 75 = ₹18 lakh; contracts = (1.5 crore × 1.2) ÷ 18 lakh = 10.
Introduction to Forwards and Futures
An investor holds shares of a company and fears a short-term fall in price but does not want to sell the shares. Using futures, she should:
Buy futures on that stock
Buy call options on an unrelated stock
Sell futures on that stock
Do nothing, as futures cannot hedge shares
A short futures position gains when the price falls, offsetting the loss on the shares.
Introduction to Forwards and Futures
On expiry, open positions in single-stock futures on Indian exchanges are settled by:
Cash settlement only
Automatic rollover to the next month
Physical delivery of the shares
Delivery of an index basket
Stock derivatives in India moved to compulsory physical settlement, while index derivatives remain cash settled.
Introduction to Options
Stock options and index options traded on Indian exchanges are of which style?
American
Bermudan
European
Asian
All equity options on Indian exchanges can be exercised only on the expiry day.
Introduction to Options
A trader buys a put (lot 1,000 shares) with strike ₹500 at a premium of ₹12. At expiry the stock settles at ₹470. His net profit is:
Introduction to Options
The maximum potential loss for the writer of a naked (uncovered) call option is:
The premium received
The strike price
Zero
Unlimited
If the underlying rises without limit, the call writer's obligation grows without limit.
Introduction to Options
A European call with strike ₹1,000 is priced at ₹60, the stock is at ₹1,000 and the present value of the strike is ₹980. By put-call parity, the put with the same strike and expiry should be worth:
Introduction to Options
Theta of a long option position is usually negative because:
The option loses time value as expiry approaches, other things being equal
Volatility always falls over time
Interest rates fall daily
The strike price is adjusted daily
Time decay erodes the extrinsic value of options, hurting buyers and benefiting writers.
Introduction to Options
The delta of a deep in-the-money call option on a stock is close to:
A deep ITM call moves almost one-for-one with the stock because exercise is almost certain.
Introduction to Options
Gamma of an option measures:
The rate of change of delta with respect to the underlying price
The change in premium for a change in volatility
The change in premium for a change in interest rates
The change in premium per day
Gamma is the second derivative of the option price with respect to the underlying.
Introduction to Options
Other things being equal, an increase in the risk-free interest rate tends to:
Increase call values and decrease put values
Decrease call values and increase put values
Increase both call and put values
Have no effect on option values
A higher rate lowers the present value of the strike, which benefits calls (pay strike later) and hurts puts.
Introduction to Options
Implied volatility of an option is:
The historical standard deviation of past returns
The volatility that, when used in a pricing model, makes the model price equal the market premium
The volatility fixed by the exchange
The difference between the high and low price of the day
Implied volatility is backed out from market prices and reflects the market's expectation of future volatility.
Strategies using Equity Futures and Options
An investor who owns shares and sells call options on them to earn premium income is using a:

All trading in the stock's cash market stops
Only trades that reduce existing positions are allowed
Only new positions can be created
Options on the stock are cancelled

Each buyer individually
The company whose stock is the underlying
The client's broker
